solutions.check: 30 entries verified against the grid (lengths, crossings, linked-clue mapping)

clue.text: "Teat tweaked by politician getting tense" crack

indicators.note: something tweaked has been twisted out of its usual shape, so the letters are pulled into a new order

blocks.note: taken as written, before rearranging
a Member of Parliament
T is the grammar abbreviation for tense

explanation.surface: A tabloid-style quote about a politician fondling a breast and getting nervous, followed by a single word.
explanation.walkthrough: The quoted sentence is all wordplay; the lone word outside it is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: To have a crack at something is to make an attempt, an informal synonym.

clue.text: Near-genital area temperature raised

blocks.note: T is the standard abbreviation for temperature
lifted up, elevated

explanation.surface: A medical-sounding note about a hot spot in the groin region.
explanation.definitionFit: The upper leg sits right beside the groin, a cheeky descriptive paraphrase of that body part.

clue.text: House right to cut kinky sex urges?

indicators.note: kinky means twisted or bent, so the letters that follow are bent into another order
something that cuts into another goes inside it, splitting it in two

blocks.note: taken as written, then rearranged
HO is the abbreviation for house
RT is an abbreviation for right

explanation.surface: Reads as a question about whether a parliament legislating on kinky sex counts as indulging urges.
explanation.walkthrough: The rearranged EXS is split by HORT to give EXHORTS. The question mark flags that 'urges' is a verb here, not a noun about desire.
explanation.definitionFit: To exhort is to urge someone strongly to act, so 'urges' as a verb is a direct synonym.

clue.text: see 11ac.
Rough drink gets Conservative arse stuck in outskirts of Stepney

indicators.note: stuck in means lodged inside something, so these letters go within the others
the outskirts of a place are its edges, so only the outer letters of the word are kept

blocks.note: first and last letters of the place name
C is the abbreviation for Conservative
the rump is the backside

explanation.surface: A Tory's backside lodged in an East London district, apparently earning a strong drink.
explanation.walkthrough: CRUMP goes between S and Y. Stepney is a district in London's East End.
explanation.definitionFit: Scrumpy is a strong, cloudy, rough cider from the West Country, so a rough drink by description.

clue.text: Type of tank top of English female, covered in Chianti, getting pissed

indicators.note: the top of a word written down the grid is its first letter
being drunk leaves things jumbled and unsteady, so the letters are scrambled

blocks.note: its opening letter
F is the abbreviation for female
taken as written, the Italian red wine

explanation.surface: An English woman in a tank top soaked in Chianti and getting drunk.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tank top' looks like a garment, but 'tank' belongs to the definition and 'top' picks a letter.
explanation.definitionFit: The Chieftain was a British main battle tank of the Cold War era, a specific example of the vehicle.

clue.text: Out of bed, casual with love, played fast and possibly loose?

blocks.note: someone out of bed is up
a casual worker is a temp
love is zero in tennis, shaped like O

explanation.surface: Someone up from bed and casual about love, playing fast and loose with partners.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Played fast and loose' is an idiom for behaving irresponsibly, but only 'played fast' is the definition; 'and possibly loose?' is surface flourish.
explanation.definitionFit: Music described as uptempo is performed at a quick pace, so played fast.

clue.text: Pissed off CIA partly

indicators.note: off here means gone bad or out of order, so the following letters are rearranged

blocks.note: taken as written, every letter used

explanation.surface: The CIA is somewhat annoyed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pissed off' reads as one phrase meaning angry, and 'partly' looks like a hidden-word signal, but it is just more letters to rearrange.
explanation.definitionFit: Paralytic is British slang for extremely drunk, and pissed is the British slang for drunk, not angry.

clue.text: To do an Archer, sound like Daisy and keep your head down

blocks.note: Jeffrey Archer, novelist and Tory peer, was jailed for perjury
Daisy is a stock name for a cow, and cows low

explanation.surface: Advice on dodging trouble: tell porkies like a disgraced peer, moo, and stay out of sight.
explanation.walkthrough: Jeffrey Archer, a Conservative novelist and peer, was imprisoned in 2001 for perjury; Daisy is a traditional name for a cow, and a cow's moo is called lowing.
explanation.definitionFit: To lie low is to stay hidden and avoid attention, which is exactly keeping your head down.

clue.text: Royal turfed out of long-term car park space

definitions.text: Royal turfed out of long-term car park space

blocks.clueFragment: Royal turfed out of long-term car park space
blocks.note: surface reading: some VIP evicted from their airport parking bay

blocks.clueFragment: turfed out of long-term car park space
blocks.note: setter's reading: a medieval king whose bones were dug up from beneath a Leicester car park, having lain there five centuries

explanation.walkthrough: In 2012 archaeologists exhumed the remains of the last Plantagenet king from under a council car park in Leicester; 'turfed out' is literal digging and 'long-term' means 500 years.
explanation.definitionFit: The skeleton found under the Leicester car park was identified as that king, killed at Bosworth in 1485.

clue.text: (& 4dn.) Harry's not begun to get involved with potty Boris's lot

indicators.note: a name that has not begun is missing its opening letter
things that get involved with each other become tangled together, so the letters mix

blocks.note: the name taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Prince Harry, apparently mad, falling in with Boris Johnson's crowd.
explanation.walkthrough: HARRY loses its H to give ARRY, which is shuffled with POTTY. Boris Johnson was then Conservative Mayor of London.
explanation.definitionFit: Boris Johnson is a Conservative, so his political party is the one he belongs to, described by association.

clue.text: (& 13ac.) Fairytale ending missing, sadly, with homely Brenda's lot?

indicators.note: with its ending missing, a word drops its final letter
sadly suggests things have gone badly wrong, so the letters end up out of order

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A fairytale that ends badly for a homely woman's household.
explanation.walkthrough: FAIRYTALE loses its last letter, then joins HOMELY for the rearrangement. Brenda is Private Eye's long-running nickname for Queen Elizabeth II.
explanation.definitionFit: Private Eye calls the Queen Brenda, so her family is the royal household; the question mark flags the nickname.

clue.text: see 12ac.
Conservative Right lives and breathes for a turning point

blocks.note: C is the abbreviation for Conservative
R is the abbreviation for right
something that lives exists, that is, it is
likewise, to breathe is to be alive, to exist

explanation.surface: A Tory right-winger who is utterly devoted to some cause.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lives and breathes' looks like the idiom for total devotion, but each verb separately means 'exists'.
explanation.definitionFit: A crisis is the decisive moment when things must change course, a dictionary sense of turning point.

clue.text: Bank punished over rise given to tosser, ultimately

indicators.note: something punished has been knocked about, so these letters are battered into a new order
ultimately points to the very end, so only the last letter of the word is kept

blocks.note: taken as written
its final letter

explanation.surface: A bank penalised after giving a pay rise to some jerk of a banker.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bank' suggests a financial institution; here it is a store or supply.
explanation.definitionFit: A reservoir is a stock held in reserve, just as a bank of something is a stored supply to draw on.

clue.text: Blooming oil-producer makes tabloid loud and even more shallow

blocks.note: The Sun is a British tabloid newspaper
F stands for forte, loud in music
less deep, comparative of low

explanation.surface: A jab at an oil tycoon whose ownership makes a tabloid noisier and shallower still.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Blooming' reads as a mild British oath, but it means flowering.
explanation.definitionFit: The plant flowers, and its seeds are pressed for a widely used cooking oil.

clue.text: Private Eye 'A' tour managed to get one knackered

indicators.note: managed suggests something handled and reorganised, so the letters are rearranged

blocks.note: the magazine speaks of itself in the editorial first person plural
taken as written, before rearranging

explanation.surface: The magazine running a tour that leaves someone exhausted.
explanation.definitionFit: To wear someone out is to exhaust them; knackered is British slang for worn out or very tired.

clue.text: As a new US president used to be squeezed by Vice?

indicators.note: being squeezed by something means being pressed inside it

blocks.note: a vice is a sin
second-hand clothes are used or worn

explanation.surface: A newly elected president once squeezed by his own Vice-President, with a hint of scandal.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Vice' looks like the Vice-President, but here it is plain wrongdoing.
explanation.definitionFit: A new US president takes the oath of office at the inauguration, so he is formally installed by oath.

clue.text: Newspaper possibly want's Nick's guts – it's only natural

indicators.note: guts are the insides, so only the middle letters of the name are kept

blocks.note: a newspaper can be the organ of a party or cause
the inner two letters

explanation.surface: A newspaper apparently craving some Nick's innards, then calling it natural.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Want's' is printed with a stray apostrophe; it reads as 'wants', joining the two parts.
explanation.definitionFit: Organic produce is grown without synthetic chemicals, the sense in which food is described as wholly natural.

clue.text: Untidy constitution exposed state

indicators.note: a constitution is how something is made up, so the letters are made up into a fresh arrangement

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A messy national constitution has been revealed for what it is.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Constitution' and 'state' look political; one rearranges letters, the other is a condition.
explanation.definitionFit: Nudity is the condition of being naked, a state in which the body is uncovered.

clue.text: Hardly an expert, on reflection, our pointless Business Secretary

indicators.note: a reflection shows things back to front, so the word is read the other way
pointless means without a point, and N is a compass point to be dropped

blocks.note: taken as written, then turned round
Vince Cable was Business Secretary in the coalition government

explanation.surface: A dig at the Business Secretary of the day as an amateur, his ideas going nowhere.
explanation.walkthrough: VINCE drops N, a compass point, to give VICE. Vince Cable, a Liberal Democrat, ran the Business department from 2010.
explanation.definitionFit: A novice is a beginner, someone with little experience, so far from being an expert.

clue.text: Flagship bad practice: drug-dropping politician

indicators.note: dropping the drug means removing the letter that stands for ecstasy

blocks.note: a vice is a bad habit
E is ecstasy
a Conservative

explanation.surface: A flagship policy exposed as bad practice by a politician giving up drugs.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Flagship' suggests a headline policy; it is Nelson's ship at Trafalgar, now preserved at Portsmouth.
explanation.definitionFit: HMS Victory was Nelson's flagship and remains the flagship of the First Sea Lord.

clue.text: German woman, common female, dismissing, at the outset, Angela Merkel's sort of economic approach?

definitions.note: an adjective; 'sort of economic approach' describes a kind of policy

indicators.note: the outset is the beginning, so only the first letter of the name is used
dismissing means sending away, so a letter is removed from the word

blocks.note: the German word for a woman or wife
the opening letter
a casual, colloquial word for a girl

explanation.surface: A sketch of Angela Merkel's thrifty economics during the euro crisis.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Angela' does double duty: its initial is the letter dropped, and the whole name belongs to the definition's picture of the German Chancellor.
explanation.definitionFit: Merkel was known for insisting on austerity and balanced budgets, a thrifty, sparing stance.

clue.text: Feed off the film actress's shit

indicators.note: off suggests spoilt or out of order, so the letters are scrambled

blocks.note: taken as written, then rearranged
Cate Blanchett, the film actress

explanation.surface: Someone ordered to eat the film star's excrement.
explanation.definitionFit: To defecate is to empty the bowels, the formal word for the vulgar verb.

clue.text: (& 27ac.) How you have to take a bitter pill? (Police numbers cut)

definitions.text: How you have to take a bitter pill?

blocks.note: a police force
when numbers are cut, they are down

explanation.surface: A grim remark about swallowing bad news, with an aside about cuts to police staffing.
explanation.walkthrough: The bracketed aside looks like commentary but is the wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: A nasty-tasting pill has to be swallowed with effort, and the phrasal verb means to swallow reluctantly.

clue.text: Starts to turf out Livingstone (of no real value)?

indicators.note: the starts of words are their opening letters, so each word gives its first letter

blocks.note: opening letters of both words
Ken Livingstone, former Mayor of London

explanation.surface: A campaign to oust Ken Livingstone, dismissed as a worthless figure.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Turf out' looks like the action against Livingstone, but only its initials count.
explanation.definitionFit: A token gesture is merely symbolic, done for show and carrying little genuine worth.

clue.text: see 25dn.
Wow! Almost starkers – unusual, laughable means of taking piss out of the system

definitions.text: means of taking piss out of the system

indicators.note: almost means nearly all, so the word loses its final letter
something unusual and laughable is odd and absurd, so the letters are made strange

blocks.note: taken as written
starkers is British slang for naked

explanation.surface: Someone nearly naked gives a surprised whoop at something ridiculous involving mockery.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Taking the piss' is British slang for mocking, but here it is literal: the urinary tract.
explanation.definitionFit: The waterworks is a jocular term for the urinary system, which drains urine from the body.

clue.text: Get rough rope wrapped round arsehole

indicators.note: rough means roughly handled or disordered, so the letters are jumbled
wrapping round something encloses it inside

blocks.note: taken as written, then rearranged
a cur is a contemptible person

explanation.surface: An order to grab some rough rope and tie up a contemptible person.
explanation.definitionFit: To procure is to obtain or acquire, a formal synonym for getting something.

clue.text: Labour leader's back, extremely narky with elected 'grand' doing what accused politicians invariably do?

definitions.text: doing what accused politicians invariably do?

indicators.note: a leader's back means the name is taken from the back, read right to left
the extremes of a word are its ends, so only the first and last letters are kept

blocks.note: Ed Miliband led the Labour Party at the time
first and last letters
a candidate elected is in
G is short for grand, a thousand pounds

explanation.surface: The Labour leader turning his back on a grumpy MP accused of taking a thousand-pound backhander.
explanation.walkthrough: Ed Miliband was Labour leader in 2013; 'a grand' is British slang for a thousand pounds.
